en: She sliced away
One skirt of the wastrel’s robe.
“Let the wrestlers seize her!”
“The shameless shrew who turned the people
Against us has devoured us!”
“A wounded boar will never recover!”
So Kanchoro went about shouting:
“She will not leave you alive!”
The valiant Kanchoro
Rallied the warriors and made ready;
From her flank, brave Kyyaz
Stood raging and poised to spring.
Your sister-in-law stood alone against that multitude—
What could the poor woman do?
How could she prevail against them?
Will seven wolves leave
Even the carcass of a single sheep?
When the Jediger swarm upon a woman
And beat her, will they leave even her remains?
They plundered her camp and disgraced her;
They brought your prince, brave Semetey,
To a wretched end,
Before your sister-in-law, a woman all alone.
She charged in fury
And was reaching for Zulpukor,
About to bring upon the warriors
Yet another slaughter,
When Kyyaz, whose battle-axe had a steel haft,
In the blink of an eye,
Before anyone could say a word,
Reached her with practiced skill
And hewed straight through the steel
At the middle of its haft.
The moon-faced woman Aichürök
Fought without rest for six days,
And suffered wounds in seven places;
She fought without rest for seven days,
And suffered wounds in seven places.
Blood flowed from her white breast;
The strength drained away
From fair Chürök, and she grew faint.
Her heroic arm, once quick to strike,
Hung powerless and numb;
Her crimson dress and fine robe
Were soaked in dark, clotted blood.
This dog-born, faithless world
Grew too narrow to contain her soul.
The noble-born Aichürök,
Parted from her hero,
Was thus brought to disgrace;
She yearned for just one glimpse
Of the mighty slayer whose life had passed.
All the Jediger
Gathered their strongest wrestlers;
Their most capable and formidable warriors
Surrounded your poor, sea-hearted sister-in-law
On every side.
They bound her hands and feet,
And the Jediger tied up
The moon-faced lady Chürök.
They mounted her on a dapple-gray pacer
And dressed her in ash-colored silk,
Saying, “Here is the perfect bride,
The mate ordained by God.”
Many warriors called her an infidel,
And said she was a widow to be taken.
They divided gold by the bowlful
And gave radiant Chürök,
The noble-born bringer of turmoil,
To brave Kyyaz.
Unable to break free, however she struggled,
Aichürök fell into their snare;
Brave Kyyaz, lord of the Jediger,
Took Aichürök away by force.
As Chürök sobbed and wept,
There was no swift steed for her to mount,
And no kinsman to rescue her.
Her waist tightly bound,
The legacy left by the slain hero
Was parted from the land of Talas
And separated from the Kyrgyz people.
Brave Kyyaz of the Jediger
Took red-tailed elephants,
Loaded the furs and gold,
Placed Aichürök at their head,
And took a thousand of the fairest women.
He destroyed the royal camp and seized its spoils,
And, when counted, took this multitude of lives.
Every capable Jediger
Took six thousand horses,
While even the poorest fool
Took some six hundred horses.
There was so much gold and silver
That they could not load it all;
So many noble brides and lovely girls
That they could not carry them all away.
Their hearts were content;
The Jediger filled the Seven Valleys,
Each gaining all he desired.
Brave Kyyaz, son of Agysh,
Became khan of the Jediger,
Ruling the people and governing the realm;
He now enjoyed every pleasure.
All of Semetey’s wealth
He measured out with a whip and divided.
His tent covering gleamed with fat;
The triumphant Kyyaz became khan,
And his heroic heart was at ease.
He made the fortified palace his dwelling,
And made Semetey, Bakay, and Külchoro—
Those three—the foundation of his fortune.
In Talas he made Kanchoro
Khan to govern the people.
The nation clamored and the people seethed,
While for that hero Kanchoro
They devised honors beyond imagining.
They held a feast for many days,
Placed a golden crown upon him,
And seated him on a golden throne,
Setting him above
The Argyn and the Kyrgyz.
That hero Kanchoro
Had Semetey’s name erased
And Kanchoro’s name proclaimed.
The towering Karakyr
Was called the domain of Khan Kanchoro;
The Argyn and Kyrgyz subjects
Were called the people of Khan Kanchoro;
Kapka and Kan-Jailak
Were called the mountains of Khan Kanchoro;
Kara-Buura and Great Chatkal
Were called the gateway of Khan Kanchoro.
Kanchoro, now seated on the throne,
And brave Kyyaz—those two—
Divided the plunder between them.
They brought a white-gray mare for sacrifice,
And without felling the mare,
Slaughtered her while she stood.
When black blood flowed from the mare,
They dipped their hands in it for their oath.
Those wretches, swaggering,
Made their covenant,
Binding the promise firmly
With a pledge punishable by death:
To pursue claims together,
Kanchoro and brave Kyyaz,
And to fight their enemies together.
“If you encamp throughout Kyrka-Tash
From the Seven Valleys,
And I encamp along the slopes
Of Kapka-Tash in broad Talas,
No mortal man will break through.
If we unite as one,
No cold-hearted foe can invade,
And no enemy can suddenly strike us,”
They said.
The two giants clasped hands,
Saying, “Agreed, agreed.”
They declared the seven forefathers
Of whoever broke these words accursed.
They chewed grains of white wheat;
The two babbled their formulas
Holding the sacred Quran,
They cut a switch and gave their word,
Making a covenant no man could escape.
“The Jediger in the Seven Valleys,
All the people who cover the earth—
My kinsman, I shall withhold none from you!”
Thus spoke brave Kyyaz:
“May I become lower than a beast;
Take my bay racehorse,
And if you desire my servitude,
Do not spare me—take my life!
My dear Kanchoro,
Spare one of us and take the other;
Leave my sibling, but take my household!
Take my low-lying land of the Seven Valleys!
Take my people, who are like the Jediger!
Take my bright red-tailed elephants;
Spare me torment—take my life and tongue!
I have spoken weighty words; understand them!
But beware of your Argyn
And Kyrgyz on this side!
There is deceit in their words,
My friend, and corruption
Can be seen in your people’s eyes.
What if we drive this nation out
In a clamorous procession?
What if, my friend, we destroy this people,
Slaughtering every man and leaving none?”
When brave Kyyaz spoke these words,
The hulking Kanchoro
Started in alarm and said:
“What manner of words are these?
Jylgyn, Keng-Kol, and Talas—
If I wish to reap them, I shall reap them;
If I wish to swallow them, I shall raise an uproar,
Gulping them down like a dragon,
And devour every last person.
If my terrible rage seizes me,
I shall leave not even a hair
And massacre this people;
If I roar in fury—”
Your people flee in terror,
Your voice is heard far and wide;
When I charge in fury,
Horses tumble over one another.
They have no strength to attack,
No power to meet me in combat;
When I shout, none among them has courage.
There is no one to rouse the people and stir the nation—
No Sary Khan or Bakay Khan.
These people will not even move;
They are as countless as slaughtered dogs,
Yet have no mettle to attack,
No strength to wrestle,
No might to grapple.
When they hear my roar,
They abandon the foe and amble away;
When I grow angry, these people
Take shelter in their homes.
When I roar in wrath,
Their hearts utterly fail,
And they begin to quake;
They readily forsake
Not only their livestock, but their lives.
Listen, my friend Kyyaz,
I have a grievance to tell my lord.
Yesterday, on the plains of Zhylgyn and Keng-Kol,
Along broad Talas,
At Kara-Buura and Batkal,
When the Kyrgyz lay spread across the land,
Camping on the hills and settling the country,
When Argyn and Kyrgyz tethered their mares,
When they had made camp,
And there was merriment by day and games by night,
In those days,
When the bored went hunting deer,
And those who were not bored
Sported freely among the people,
Growing merry on kumis,
Wiping sweat from their brows,
After drinking their liquor,
We could find no mountain to assail,
No enemy to fight;
In Talas we stood raging,
Eager for any foe who ventured near,
Breaking through rock to make roads,
Laying waste to many lands,
While we held them besieged—
Had word of this reached you?—
We had girded our waists firmly.
From the Chinese khan of Beijing
We pursued the blood-price of mighty Manas.
From the banks of Kara-Suu,
From the plain of Kaspan-Too,
